The process

Four steps from quote to driveway

Most people have never shipped a car before. Here is exactly what happens, in order, so nothing catches you off guard.

Get your number

Price your route above or call dispatch. The range you see reflects what carriers are actually accepting on that lane this week — not a lowball figure we raise later.

Takes about a minute

We assign a carrier

We post your route and match it to a vetted hauler. We check their authority and cargo insurance against FMCSA records before anyone touches your vehicle. Only then does payment come up.

Usually 1–3 days

Pickup and inspection

The driver calls ahead, walks the vehicle with you, and records its condition on the bill of lading. You both sign. That document is what protects you if anything is disputed later.

You pick the window
04

Delivery and sign-off

The driver calls when they're close. You inspect against the pickup report, sign, and pay the carrier the balance — cash, certified funds, or whatever you agreed at booking. If something looks wrong, do not sign a clean bill of lading; note it, photograph it, and call us before the truck leaves.

Why brokers differ

What you actually get for the broker fee

Anyone can post a load. The difference is who gets vetted, who answers at 7pm, and whether the price holds.

The price holds

Your booked rate is locked for 30 days. If the lane moves against us, that is our problem, not a surcharge on your invoice.

Carriers get checked

We pull active authority and cargo coverage from FMCSA before dispatch. No coverage, no load — regardless of how fast they can be there.

Nothing due up front

You pay when a carrier is assigned and pickup is scheduled. If we never dispatch, you never pay a cent.

One person owns your file

You get a named coordinator, not a queue. Same person from quote through delivery, reachable seven days a week.

A deep carrier board

Access to thousands of vetted haulers nationwide means rural pickups and awkward lanes still get covered, not sat on.

Paperwork that protects you

Condition reports at both ends, photographed and signed. If a claim ever comes up, you have the documentation to win it.

Reachable hours

Dispatch runs Monday to Saturday, 8am–7pm Eastern, and someone monitors the board outside those hours for active loads.

Straight answers

If your lane is hard or your budget is unrealistic, we say so at quote time rather than taking the booking and stalling.

Ways we move vehicles

Pick the service that fits the car

Door-to-door

The truck comes to your address, not a terminal. If the street can't take a 75-foot rig, the driver meets you at a nearby lot — a grocery store or shopping centre a few minutes away.

Open carrier

The standard eight to ten car hauler you see on the interstate. It is how dealerships move new inventory, and it is what roughly nine in ten of our customers choose.

Enclosed carrier

A sealed trailer, usually two to seven cars, often with a hydraulic lift gate for low clearance. Worth the premium for anything collectible, freshly restored, or six figures.

Expedited

A guaranteed pickup date instead of a window. We pay above market to pull a driver onto your lane, so it costs more — but the date holds.

Cross-country

Coast to coast on the major freight corridors. Long lanes have the best per-mile economics, so a 2,800-mile move often costs less than twice a 900-mile one.

Fleet and commercial

Multi-unit moves for dealers, auctions, rental branches, and corporate relocations. Volume pricing and a dedicated coordinator on the account.

Before you book

Three things worth knowing

Short, practical, and written by the people who dispatch these loads. No sign-up required.

Prep · 5 min read

Getting your car ready

Fifteen minutes of prep prevents most delivery disputes. The bill of lading is only as good as the condition of the car when it's written.

  • Wash it — dirt hides scratches the inspection needs to catch
  • Photograph all four corners, roof and odometer in daylight
  • Leave a quarter tank of fuel, no more
  • Remove toll tags, parking passes and loose trim
  • Fold mirrors, disable the alarm, hand over one key
Risk · 4 min read

Spotting a bad broker

The auto transport market has a low barrier to entry, and the cheapest quote is usually the one that never gets covered.

  • A quote far under everyone else is bait — it gets raised or stalls
  • Large deposit demanded before a carrier is assigned
  • No MC or DOT number shown, or one that fails FMCSA lookup
  • Refuses to name the carrier once your load is dispatched
  • Only reachable by text and never the same person twice
Timing · 4 min read

When you ship changes the price

Auto transport is a live freight market. The same route can swing several hundred dollars depending on the week you book it.

  • January to March: northbound out of Florida runs expensive
  • Late spring through summer: peak volume, book earlier
  • Snowbird season inverts pricing on north–south lanes
  • Rural pickups wait longer than interstate-adjacent ones
  • A flexible ready date is worth real money on a hard lane

Questions

Answers before you commit

How much does it cost to ship a car?
Distance, vehicle size, whether it runs, and open versus enclosed. Per-mile rates fall as distance rises — roughly $1.45 a mile under 300 miles, about $1.00 at 600 miles, and near $0.57 coast to coast. A running sedan on an open carrier from Chicago to Miami lands around $950 to $1,100. Price your specific route for a real range.
When do I pay, and how?
Nothing is charged until a carrier is assigned and pickup is scheduled. At that point you pay the broker fee, and the balance goes to the driver at delivery — cash, certified funds, or whatever you agreed at booking. If we never dispatch a carrier, you never pay.
How long will it take?
Pickup is typically 1 to 5 days after dispatch depending on the lane. Transit is roughly 1 to 3 days under 500 miles, 2 to 5 days for 500 to 1,500 miles, and 5 to 10 days coast to coast. Weather, road closures, and DOT hours-of-service rules can move these. You get an estimated window before you book, not after.
Is my vehicle insured during transport?
Yes. Every carrier we dispatch carries active cargo insurance, and we verify it against FMCSA records before assigning your vehicle. Your own policy generally still applies as well. Personal belongings left in the car are not covered by cargo insurance.
Can I leave items in the car?
Up to about 100 pounds in the trunk, below the window line. It is not covered by cargo insurance, it adds weight the carrier is liable for at weigh stations, and some carriers refuse it outright. Keep it light and keep anything valuable with you.
What does the price guarantee actually cover?
Your booked rate is locked for 30 days from booking. If carrier rates on your lane rise in that window, we absorb the difference rather than passing it to you. It does not cover changes you make — a new pickup address, a switch from open to enclosed, or a vehicle that turns out not to run will be re-quoted.
Can you ship a car that doesn't run?
Yes, but it needs a carrier with a winch, and it must roll, brake, and steer. Expect roughly $150 to $200 above the running rate. Tell us at quote time — discovering it at pickup means the driver leaves without the car and you go back on the board.
Do you pick up from auctions?
Regularly — Manheim, ADESA, Copart, and IAAI nationwide. Send the lot number, buyer ID, and gate pass details when you book. Worth noting that auction storage fees start accruing fast, so book the transport the same day you win the lot.
What if my car is damaged in transit?
Note it on the bill of lading before the driver leaves, photograph it, and call us the same day. That signed condition report from pickup is what makes a claim work. Sign a clean delivery receipt and the claim becomes very hard to win — so inspect properly, even in the dark, even in the rain.
Can I track my vehicle?
Once dispatched, you get the carrier's direct contact and we check in on the load. Most owner-operators do not run consumer-facing GPS, so tracking is a phone call rather than a map pin. Anyone promising live GPS on every load is overselling how this industry works.
